analysis.one_liner: Triples the tax credit employers can claim for providing child care, with bigger breaks for small firms and rural areas.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 1, 2025 with one cosponsor and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has received no vote or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law lets employers claim a tax credit for 25% of what they spend building or running child care for their workers' kids. This bill raises that to 40% for all employers, 50% for businesses with 500 or fewer employees, and 60% for facilities in low-income census tracts or rural counties, and raises the annual dollar caps to $1.2 million. It also directs the Treasury Department to publicize the credit and orders a government study of state licensing rules that make it hard for child care providers, especially multi-state ones, to participate.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers that pay for child care get a larger tax credit — up to 60% of their costs, capped at $1.2 million a year per business. Workers benefit only indirectly: a family gets help only if its employer decides to build, run, or pay for child care, and the bill does not require any employer to do so.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Participating employers and, indirectly, their workers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the employer-provided child care credit from 25% of qualified costs to a 40% baseline, 50% for small businesses with 500 or fewer employees, and 60% for facilities in low-income census tracts or rural counties [S2].
Raises the yearly caps from $600,000 in credit against $1 million in costs (current law) to $1.2 million in credit against $2 million in expenditures [S2].
Requires Treasury to run a public awareness program so employers know the credit exists and how to claim it [S2].

Directs the Government Accountability Office to study state licensing and regulatory barriers on child care providers and recommend changes, including for multi-employer and multi-state facilities [S2].
Directs Treasury guidance on multi-employer child care facilities, which current rules make difficult to structure [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost through forgone revenue. The bill does not cap total claims nationally, so the cost depends on how many employers use the enlarged credit.

drawbacks.text: A worker's child care benefit depends entirely on their employer choosing to participate. Workers at firms that opt out, part-time workers, the unemployed, and anyone switching jobs get nothing [S2].
A tax credit partly reimburses spending employers would have made anyway, so some of the revenue cost buys no new child care; the bill adds no requirement that participation expand access [S2].

By enlarging a credit that flows only through employers, the bill deepens the job-based channel for child care, leaving families without a participating employer — often lower-wage workers — further behind [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A higher credit could push more employers into the child care business, especially the 50% and 60% rates aimed at small firms and rural and low-income areas, and it addresses real barriers — many employers never claim the existing credit. But the help reaches families only through their job, leaves out everyone else, and some of the cost subsidizes spending that would have happened anyway. It is a targeted, job-tied subsidy rather than broad child care relief.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sits with the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it since it was referred in May 2025.

narrative.text: Representative David Kustoff, a Republican, introduced the bill with Representative Claudia Tenney on May 1, 2025 [S1] [S2].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S4].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote has been recorded; the complete action history ends with the committee referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no vote taken, no one has gained or lost yet. Employers keep the current smaller 25% credit unchanged, and families waiting for more child care options see no change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No change yet; employers keep current law

for.name: Rep. David Kustoff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise and expand the employer-provided child care credit.

for.name: Rep. Claudia Tenney
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republicans are on record supporting the bill, and no one has spoken or voted against it; it has never advanced past a committee referral [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill deepens the employer's role as the tax-favored channel for child care, reimbursing up to 60% of their costs. Families benefit only if their employer opts in, so the employer's tax gain does not automatically become a family's gain.

industries.industry: Child care providers and facility operators
industries.note: Employer-funded facilities mean new customers and revenue for providers. The bill's GAO study targets licensing rules and multi-state barriers that limit provider participation.
The bill specifically requires Treasury guidance on multi-employer facilities and directs the GAO to recommend reducing barriers for multi-state operators seeking the credit.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor and no committee action after referral, the bill is unlikely to move on its own this Congress. Its only realistic path is being folded into a larger tax package the Ways and Means Committee drafts, which requires its sponsors to win a spot among competing tax proposals.
